opus-5.5.text:
For me, open source has never really felt like a strategy. It's closer to how I learned to do research in the first place. When I started out, almost everything I built on came from people who had put their code, papers, and ideas out there for free. So contributing back feels less like generosity and more like part of a cycle I've always been inside.

One thing I've come to appreciate is that sharing your work openly changes the work itself. When you know other people will run your code, read it, and break it in ways you never imagined, you build differently. You care more about clean abstractions and about whether something actually holds up in real use, not just in a paper benchmark. And the feedback loop is incredibly fast. Someone you've never met files an issue or sends a pull request, and suddenly the project is better than anything you could have built alone.

There's also a community side to it that I really value. Some of the most meaningful collaborations I've had started with strangers who found a project, got excited, and just started contributing. Many of them were students or engineers with no formal connection to us. Open source lowers the barrier for people to join, and that matters a lot to me, because I remember what it felt like to be on the outside looking in.

That said, I don't think open source is automatically good in every situation, and it isn't free. Maintaining a project is a lot of work: reviewing code, answering questions, keeping things stable while still moving fast. You have to think about sustainability, about how to support the people doing that work, and about being responsible with what you release. But overall, I believe progress, especially in AI systems, moves faster and more fairly when knowledge is shared. If the infrastructure is open, more people get to build on it, question it, and improve it. That's the kind of ecosystem I want to help create.

r001.rationale: Saying open source never felt like a strategy and was part of a cycle Ying had always been inside characterizes the relationship as natural rather than deliberately pursued.

r002.rationale: The response says Ying learned from people who shared code, papers, and ideas, but it does not clearly identify those people as anonymous or describe them as formative teachers.

r003.rationale: The response values sharing and discusses its benefits, but does not say that withholding Ying’s own ideas or creations feels strange.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think for me, open source was never really a decision I made at one point—it was more like the water I grew up in. When I was a student, almost everything I learned came from reading other people's code, from papers with released implementations, from people answering questions on forums without expecting anything back. So by the time I started doing my own research, it felt natural that whatever I built should go back into that same pool.

I'd say my relationship with it has two layers. The first is practical. In systems work, especially around LLM inference, the problems are so fast-moving that no single lab or company can see the whole picture. When we opened up our work on things like SGLang, the most valuable thing we got wasn't recognition—it was people hitting bugs we never would have hit, bringing workloads we never would have imagined, and sometimes contributing fixes better than what we would have written ourselves. Open source is, in a very real sense, the fastest way to make the work good.

The second layer is more personal. I genuinely believe that the sharing culture is what makes this field feel like a community rather than a race. There's a kind of trust in it—you put something out before it's perfect, you let people see your mistakes, and in exchange you get to stand on everyone else's work too. I've benefited enormously from that generosity, so I feel a responsibility to keep it going, especially now that so much of AI is moving behind closed doors.

That said, I don't think of it as purely idealistic. Openness has to be sustainable. Maintainers burn out, companies need to make money, and some things really are sensitive. So I try to be thoughtful about what to open, when, and how to build a community around it rather than just dropping code and walking away. But my default is still to share, and I hope it stays that way.

r001.rationale: Ying says open source was not a decision made at one point; it was “the water I grew up in,” and sharing her work felt natural.

r002.rationale: She credits others’ code, released implementations, and forum answers with shaping what she learned, but does not say those contributors were anonymous.

r003.rationale: She says it felt natural to share her work, but does not clearly convey that withholding an idea or creation from others feels strange.

astra-6.text:
For me, open source is a way of learning together. You share something you’ve built, other people try it, question your assumptions, and sometimes take it in a direction you hadn’t imagined. That exchange can be just as valuable as the code itself.

I think the culture of sharing depends on making that participation feel welcome. Publishing your work is one step; explaining your decisions, being open to criticism, and helping someone understand how to contribute are part of it too. You don’t have to have a perfect solution before you have something worth sharing.

r001.rationale: The response describes open source as collaborative learning, but does not say the relationship developed naturally rather than through deliberate commitment.

r002.rationale: It does not mention anonymous people sharing programming resources online or identify them as formative teachers.

r003.rationale: It supports sharing and welcoming participation, but does not convey that keeping an idea or creation to oneself feels strange.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of open source as a reciprocal relationship. So much of what we’re able to build depends on knowledge, tools, and code that other people have shared. When you benefit from that, contributing back feels natural.

And sharing isn’t only about publishing code. It’s also about explaining your thinking, documenting what didn’t work, and making it easier for someone else to get started. That process helps you understand your own work better, too, because other people ask questions you might never have considered.

To me, the most valuable part of that culture is the idea that you don’t have to solve everything alone. You can build on someone else’s work, contribute something of your own, and let the next person take it further.

r001.rationale: It says contributing back feels natural, but does not say Ying Sheng’s relationship with open source developed naturally rather than through a deliberate commitment.

r002.rationale: It mentions benefiting from others’ shared knowledge, tools, and code, but does not identify anonymous online programmers as formative teachers.

r003.rationale: It describes sharing as valuable and contributing back as natural, but does not convey that withholding an idea or creation feels strange.
